title: Thermodynamics for engineers
note: First law: energy is conserved, ΔU = Q − W (heat added minus work done by the system). Second law: heat flows on its own only from hot to cold, and no engine turns all its heat into work. Carnot efficiency 1 − T_c/T_h, with kelvin temperatures, is the upper limit for any engine between two temperatures.

read.title: The limit on every engine
text: A power plant, a car engine, and a jet all do the same job: take in heat at a high temperature, turn part of it into work, and dump the rest at a lower temperature. The first law keeps the books. Work out plus heat rejected equals heat in, so a 30% efficient engine that takes in 1000 J delivers 300 J of work and rejects 700 J.

The second law sets the ceiling. Building on Sadi Carnot's work of the 1820s, physicists showed that no engine running between a hot reservoir at T_h and a cold one at T_c can beat 1 − T_c/T_h, with temperatures in kelvin. An engine between 600 K and 300 K can never exceed 50%, however well it is built. To do better, engineers raise the hot temperature, which is why turbine blades are made of exotic alloys and cooled from inside.

Run the cycle backward and you get a refrigerator or heat pump. Work drives heat from cold to hot. Because the device moves heat rather than creating it, a heat pump can deliver three or four joules of heat to a house for each joule of electricity.
Heat moves by conduction through solids, convection in moving fluids, and radiation, which needs no medium at all.
